Where it began

Mohinder Amarnath was born in Patiala on 24 September 1950, into one of Indian cricket's best-known families. His father was Lala Amarnath, India's first captain after independence. His elder brother Surinder also played international cricket, and his younger brother Rajinder played first-class cricket. He went to school in Delhi and took his degree at SGTB Khalsa College, part of Delhi University.

The player

He first played for India in December 1969, against Australia at Chennai, as an all-rounder who bowled at a lively pace. Six years passed before he was picked again, and when he returned it was as a batsman, usually at number three. His first Test hundred came at the WACA in Perth against Jeff Thomson, and in 1976 his 85 in the second innings at Port of Spain took India to within touching distance of a famous win. In 69 Tests to 1988 he scored 4,378 runs, averaging 42.50 with 11 centuries; he also took 32 wickets.

The season of 1982–83 was his finest. In 11 Tests against Pakistan and West Indies he made more than 1,000 runs, and he shared the man of the series award in Pakistan with Imran Khan. At the 1983 World Cup, as India's vice-captain, he was man of the match in both the semi-final and the final. In the final he batted patiently for 26 against a fearsome West Indies attack, then took 3 for 12 from seven overs, including the last wicket, as India won their first world title.

What made him special

Fast bowling never frightened him. In an age of bouncers he kept on hooking, however often he was hit, and players and pundits often name him as India's finest batsman against genuine pace. Imran Khan rated him the best batsman in the world in 1982–83, and Sunil Gavaskar paid him a similar tribute. With the ball he bowled swing and cutters with fine control, off an unusual run-up that slowed as he neared the crease.

His Test place was rarely secure for long, but each time he lost it he made his way back through weight of runs, which is how he came to be called the Comeback Man of Indian cricket.

Away from the middle

Around the end of his playing days he presented a weekly coaching programme on Doordarshan, Cricket with Mohinder Amarnath, and one of the young players he interviewed was a 15-year-old Sachin Tendulkar. He went on to work as a cricket analyst. He was named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year and won the Arjuna Award, and in 2009 the Indian board gave him its highest honour for a former player, the C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award. He appeared in the 2021 film 83, about the World Cup win, in which he played his own father.

And finally

He always batted with a red handkerchief showing in his trouser pocket. He also has the rare distinction of having been out in international cricket both for handling the ball and for obstructing the field, the only man to collect that pair. Even his dismissals were original.
